title: MECE Framework
subtitle: Structure any problem so nothing overlaps and nothing is missed
useWhen: You're presenting an analysis, making a recommendation, or solving a complex problem and your thinking feels incomplete, repetitive, or hard to follow. You need a structure that is airtight.
howToUse: MECE stands for Mutually Exclusive, Collectively Exhaustive. It is a McKinsey core thinking principle. Mutually Exclusive means every category is distinct, no overlap. Collectively Exhaustive means together the categories cover everything, no gaps. When your problem breakdown is MECE, your analysis is complete, your communication is clear, and your solution covers all the ground. AI can test whether your structure is MECE and help rebuild it if it isn't.
steps: Define the problem or decision you need to structure.
Ask AI to break it into MECE categories and check for overlaps or gaps.
Use the MECE structure as your analysis framework and your presentation outline.

Apply MECE to any situation where you need to be sure nothing is missed. Barbara Minto created MECE at McKinsey in the 1960s to solve a specific problem: consultant reports were being rejected because the logic had gaps or overlaps. She codified the principle that categories must not repeat (mutually exclusive) and together must cover everything (collectively exhaustive). It became the backbone of all McKinsey output and the standard for structured thinking in consulting globally. ORIGIN STORY
origin: McKinsey & Company — core consulting methodology, attributed to Barbara Minto, 1960s
promptBody:
Act as a McKinsey-trained strategy consultant.
Problem or question to structure: [YOUR PROBLEM, DECISION, OR ANALYSIS TOPIC]
Step 1       :    Break this into MECE categories. Each category must be 
                       distinct,  no overlap. Together they must cover everything, no gaps.
Step 2      :    Check your structure. Flag any overlaps or missing areas.
Step 3      :    For each category, list the 2–3 key questions I need to answer to 
                       address it completely.
Format as a structured outline I can use directly.
